item.title: Gibraltar imaged by IRIDE Eaglet II
item.summary: Image: While the final eight IRIDE Eaglet II satellites were launched a week ago, the first images from Eaglet II satellites launched earlier are being returned, including a view of Gibraltar featured here.
item.page_text:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
While the final eight IRIDE Eaglet II satellites were launched a week ago, the first images from Eaglet II satellites launched earlier are being returned, including a view of Gibraltar featured here.
Soon after launch, the satellites start acquiring and transmitting high-resolution images of the Earth. The results confirm the success of the initial in-orbit operations, the effectiveness of the systems developed, and the value of the infrastructure for applications such as port and airport monitoring and maritime traffic surveillance.
For example, this image shows Gibraltar, with the iconic Rock of Gibraltar dominating the peninsula. The densely built urban area, port facilities and airport are clearly visible, while numerous ships dot the surrounding waters.
To read more and access more of first images, see the ASI news release .
The IRIDE Eaglet II constellation, entirely designed and developed by OHB Italia and equipped with a dedicated Control Centre for satellite operations throughout all phases of the mission, was recently completed with the launch of its final eight satellites. All of them have successfully completed the Launch and Early Orbit Phase (LEOP), the first major operational milestone following launch: the satellites were successfully placed into orbit and are now ready for performance verification and subsequent entry into service.
The images, received by OHB Italia’s Control Centre in Rome, are the outcome of the satellites’ crucial commissioning phase and demonstrate the capabilities of both the platform and the optical instrument.
Like the other 16 satellites in the Eaglet II constellation, each carries a multispectral sensor, which captures images of Earth’s surface, as well as an automatic identification system to support maritime monitoring and safety services.
As well as the Eaglet II constellation, the IRIDE programme has also launched Hawk for Earth Observation (HEO) satellites. The HEO constellation carries multispectral, high-resolution optical instruments, which capture image data across multiple wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum. Argotec is responsible for developing and building the HEO satellites.
About IRIDE IRIDE is the national Earth observation infrastructure owned by the Italian Space Agency (ASI), developed under the EU’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) and supplemented by the Complementary National Plan (PNC). The programme, which is developed by the European Space Agency (ESA) with the support of the Italian Space Agency (ASI), integrates satellite constellations, ground infrastructure, and digital services to transform Earth observation data into operational geospatial services that support institutions, public administration, research, and the country's economic development. Upon completion of the development and validation phase, operational responsibility for the system is progressively transferred to ASI, which oversees its operational management and evolution.

why: Fresh first-light imagery from the new IRIDE Eaglet II constellation, showing a new sensor platform in action.

It shows the Rock of Gibraltar, the dense urban area, port facilities, the airport and numerous ships in the surrounding waters. Each Eaglet II satellite carries a multispectral sensor and an automatic identification system (AIS) receiver. The constellation was built by OHB Italia, and the image was received at OHB Italia's Control Centre in Rome.

item.page_text:
Want to explore the night sky? Two new interactive maps offer very different ways to do it. Skyviewer lets you explore the vast astronomical survey being created by the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory , while Stargazing for Beginners helps you work out what you can actually see in the sky above you.
Skyviewer is an interactive window onto Rubin Observatory's survey of the cosmos. Located in Chile, Rubin will repeatedly scan the sky for the next ten years, creating an enormous time-lapse record of the changing universe. You can use Skyviewer to explore the results from these scans, navigating around Rubin's imagery to discover stars, galaxies and other celestial objects.
The experience also includes Skysynth , which turns this visual exploration into a sonified journey through the cosmos.
If Skyviewer is about exploring the universe, Stargazing for Beginners is about exploring the sky above your head. The interactive sky map uses your location and the current time to show what is visible, with a mobile orientation mode that lets you point your phone at the sky to identify objects.
You can speed up time to watch the sky change over hours or days, filter objects by type and limiting magnitude, and search for individual stars and other celestial objects. The map also includes altitude charts, twilight information and a calendar of upcoming astronomical events.
There is even an astronomical events layer showing rise and set times, lunar phases, Moon perigee and apogee, equinoxes and solstices, planetary events and conjunctions, meteor-shower peaks, eclipses and future planetary transits. You can therefore use the map not just to see what is in the sky now, but to find out what astronomical events you might be able to watch in the future.

why: Interactive Rubin Observatory survey viewer offers a visually rich, data-driven map of a large time-domain sky survey.

draft.what_it_shows: Maps Mania highlights two interactive sky maps. Skyviewer is a browser viewer for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's survey: the Chile-based observatory will repeatedly scan the sky for ten years, building a time-lapse record, and users can navigate its imagery to find stars, galaxies and other objects (Skysynth adds a sonified version). Stargazing for Beginners is a sky map driven by the user's location and current time, with a phone orientation mode, time acceleration, filters by object type and limiting magnitude, altitude charts, twilight information and an astronomical events layer.
uncertainties: Not Earth observation. This is celestial cartography and interactive web mapping, so the editor should confirm it fits the feed.
The source gives no instrument, camera, band, resolution or acquisition date for the Rubin imagery in Skyviewer. It also does not say how much of the survey is currently viewable.
The creator or publisher of Stargazing for Beginners is not named in the source, so it cannot be credited.
The source gives no direct links to Skyviewer or Stargazing for Beginners. Only the Maps Mania link is available.
The image licence is not stated and the reuse policy is link_only. No image should be attached. The page suggests 'via Maps Mania' as the credit, so Maps Mania is credited in the post text.
Rubin Observatory's social handle was not confirmed, so the name is written plainly.

posts.facebook:
Rubin Observatory will scan the same sky over and over for the next ten years, and you can pan around its imagery in a browser.

Skyviewer, from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, lets you navigate the survey to find stars, galaxies and other objects, and a Skysynth mode turns the imagery into sound. A second tool, Stargazing for Beginners, takes the opposite approach: it uses your location and the current time to show what is visible overhead, with filters for object type and limiting magnitude. Two very different takes on sky #Cartography, spotted by Maps Mania.

Read more: http://googlemapsmania.blogspot.com/2026/10/mapping-cosmos.html

posts.linkedin:
The interface patterns we use for Earth data (pan, filter by attribute, scrub through time, render for a given location) work just as well on the sky.

Maps Mania highlights two interactive sky maps. Skyviewer gives browser access to imagery from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which will repeatedly scan the sky for ten years to build a time-lapse record of the changing universe. Stargazing for Beginners is a location- and time-driven map. It uses a phone's orientation to identify objects, filters by type and limiting magnitude, and adds an events layer covering rise and set times, eclipses, conjunctions and planetary transits. For anyone building #Cartography or web GIS products, both are useful reference designs for handling a time dimension and a very large image survey in one view. One caveat: the write-up says nothing about how much of the Rubin survey Skyviewer currently holds, or about the source data behind the beginner map, so treat them as interface examples rather than data references.

Read more: http://googlemapsmania.blogspot.com/2026/10/mapping-cosmos.html
